title: 01. Fundamentals & Trade-offs: Fault Tolerance
summary: Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to continue operating correctly and providing service after one or more of its components fail, without human intervention.
objectives: What is the difference between fault tolerance and high availability?
Explain the heartbeat failure-detection mechanism and its timeout trade-off.
What is a circuit breaker, and how does it prevent cascading failures?
Explain the bulkhead pattern and why it matters for microservices.

sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** Fault tolerance is the ability of a system to continue operating correctly and providing service after one or more of its components fail, without human intervention.

Fault tolerance is the operational manifestation of resilience engineering. A non-fault-tolerant system treats any component failure as a system failure — one dead disk, one crashed process, one network blip, and the whole thing stops working. A fault-tolerant system is designed so that component failures are expected, detected, isolated, and worked around automatically, with the user-facing service continuing to behave correctly, perhaps at reduced capacity. The distinction matters because in distributed systems, partial failure is the norm, not the exception. At Amazon or Google scale — tens of thousands of machines, millions of components — something is always failing. A system that cannot tolerate failures cannot run at scale; this is why fault tolerance is one of the first non-functional requirements senior engineers consider.

Fault tolerance begins with failure detection. You cannot tolerate a failure you cannot see. The most common detection mechanism is the heartbeat: each node periodically sends a small "I'm alive" message to a monitor or its peers; if heartbeats stop arriving for longer than a timeout, the node is presumed dead. Heartbeats are simple but have an inherent trade-off: short timeouts detect failures faster but produce false positives during transient slowness (network hiccup, GC pause); long timeouts reduce false positives but increase the time before a dead node is noticed. Google Spanner uses heartbeats with adaptive timeouts that learn each node's typical latency. Cassandra and Redis Cluster use gossip protocols, where each node exchanges state with a random peer every second; failures propagate through the cluster in O(log N) rounds. Gossip is more robust than centralized heartbeating because there is no single monitor to fail, and it scales naturally.

Once a failure is detected, the system must isolate it and continue operating. The two main isolation patterns are redundancy and failover. Redundancy means running multiple copies of each component so the loss of one is invisible to users — multiple web servers behind a load balancer, multiple database replicas, multiple AZs. Failover means redirecting traffic from a failed component to a healthy one — promoting a database replica, switching to a standby, re-routing at the DNS level. Both require that the system has spare capacity to absorb the load when a component fails. The pitfall: many systems are nominally redundant but do not have enough spare capacity — running at 90% CPU on every node means a single failure pushes the survivors into overload, cascading further failures. Capacity planning for fault tolerance means provisioning for N+1 (one failure tolerated) or N+2 (one failure plus one maintenance window) at minimum.

Beyond redundancy, several patterns enable fault tolerance at the application layer. The circuit breaker monitors calls to a downstream service and, after a threshold of failures, "opens" — it stops calling the downstream and returns a fallback or error immediately, giving the downstream time to recover. Without a circuit breaker, a slow downstream causes the upstream to exhaust connection pools and threads, propagating the failure upstream in a cascading pattern. The bulkhead pattern isolates resources by partition — e.g., dedicating separate thread pools to different downstream services so that one slow service cannot starve the others. Netflix's Hystrix (now superseded by resilience4j) popularized these patterns in the Java ecosystem; they are now standard in any microservice framework. Graceful degradation extends the idea: when a dependency fails, the system serves a reduced version of the response (cached data, default values, omitted features) rather than failing entirely.

The real-world canonical example is Google Spanner. Spanner is a globally distributed relational database that provides externally consistent distributed transactions across datacenters. Its fault tolerance is built on Paxos — every shard (a "tablet") is replicated across at least three datacenters in different regions, and writes must be committed by a Paxos majority. If one datacenter fails completely (power, network, fire), the Paxos group continues operating with the surviving majority — no data loss, no inconsistency, only a brief leader election. This is what allows Spanner to advertise 99.999% availability for regional configurations: it tolerates the loss of an entire region without manual intervention. The trade-off is latency: every write requires Paxos consensus across multiple regions, adding tens of milliseconds. Spanner's design philosophy is that strong consistency and fault tolerance are worth the latency cost for the workloads it targets (AdWords, Play, Gmail metadata).

The second real-world example is Netflix's Chaos Engineering program. Netflix does not just design for fault tolerance — they actively test it in production by deliberately causing failures. Chaos Monkey terminates random production instances during business hours. Latency Monkey injects network latency between services to simulate degraded networks. Conformity Monkey flags instances that don't meet tagging or configuration standards. The Simian Army (the umbrella name) is a suite of these tools. The motivation: a system that has never been tested under failure is a system whose fault tolerance is theoretical, not proven. Many teams believe their system is fault-tolerant because they designed it that way; chaos engineering converts that belief into evidence by forcing real failures and observing whether the system continues to operate. The cultural shift is significant — engineering teams must accept that production failures are normal and design accordingly, rather than treating them as exceptional events to be prevented.

The pitfalls in fault tolerance engineering are well-known. First, shared dependencies create correlated failures — if every service depends on the same identity provider, a failure of that provider brings down every service even though each looks independently fault-tolerant on a diagram. The fix is mapping dependencies explicitly and ensuring critical paths have independent fallbacks. Second, retry storms amplify failures — when a downstream is slow, every upstream retries, multiplying load and turning a transient issue into a sustained outage. The fix is exponential backoff with jitter and circuit breakers. Third, false positives in failure detection cause unnecessary failovers — a node that is briefly slow (GC pause) is marked dead and its traffic is moved, then it recovers and you have split-brain. The fix is grace periods and lease-based leadership. Fourth, failover itself can fail — the standby has not been tested and does not actually work when promoted. The fix is regular failover drills (Netflix's Chaos Monkey extends to database failover testing). Fault tolerance is not a feature you add; it is a property that must be designed, implemented, tested, and continuously verified.

Fault tolerance connects to every other system design concept. It depends on redundancy (multiple copies), which depends on consistency (replicas must agree), which trades off with availability (the CAP theorem). It interacts with durability (a fault-tolerant storage system must not lose data on failure). It interacts with latency (synchronous replication for fault tolerance adds latency). It interacts with reliability (a fault-tolerant system is more reliable) and observability (you cannot tolerate what you cannot detect). Senior engineers treat fault tolerance as a layered defense: detection at the network and process layer, isolation at the service layer (bulkheads, circuit breakers), redundancy at the data layer (replication, quorum), and verification at the operational layer (chaos engineering, DR drills).

sections.title: Visual Explanation
sections.body:
### Mermaid Diagram
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Client
    participant L as Load Balancer
    participant A as Service A (healthy)
    participant B as Service B (failed)
    participant CB as Circuit Breaker
    participant F as Fallback Cache

    C->>L: request
    L->>A: try A
    A-->>L: 200 OK
    L-->>C: response

    Note over B: B fails (crash/timeout)
    L->>B: try B (no response)
    L->>CB: record failure
    CB-->>CB: failures > threshold -> OPEN
    L->>A: route to A only
    L->>F: fallback for B-specific data
    F-->>L: cached value
    L-->>C: degraded response

    Note over B: B recovers after 30s
    CB->>B: half-open probe
    B-->>CB: 200 OK
    CB-->>CB: CLOSE circuit
    L->>B: traffic resumes
```

### ASCII Diagram
```
                  +-----------------+
                  | Load Balancer   |
                  |  + health check |
                  +--------+--------+
                           |
              +------------+------------+
              |                         |
              v                         v
        +-----------+             +-----------+
        | Node A    |             | Node B    |   <- heartbeat stops
        | healthy   |             | DEAD      |
        +-----+-----+             +-----------+
              |
              v
   +-------------------+
   | Circuit Breaker   |   failure threshold -> OPEN
   +---------+---------+
             |
   +---------v---------+
   | Fallback / cache  |
   +-------------------+
             |
   +---------v---------+
   | Client gets       |
   | degraded response |
   +-------------------+

   After 30s: half-open probe -> if healthy, CLOSE circuit, resume traffic
```

### Walkthrough
1. The load balancer periodically health-checks each backend node (HTTP GET /health, TCP connect, custom probe). As long as a node responds within the timeout, it stays in the healthy pool and receives traffic.
2. Node B fails — process crash, OOM, hardware fault, or network partition. Its heartbeat to the load balancer stops, or its health check starts timing out. The load balancer marks B unhealthy after the configured failure threshold (typically 3 consecutive failures).
3. The load balancer stops sending new traffic to B. Surviving nodes (A and others) absorb the load. If the failure was in a downstream service rather than the node itself, the circuit breaker opens after observing repeated failures, short-circuiting further calls.
4. For requests that depend on B's specific functionality, the system returns a fallback — cached data, a default value, or a degraded response. The client experience is reduced but not broken.
5. After a recovery interval (typically 30s), the load balancer or circuit breaker probes B with a single request. If it succeeds, B is marked healthy and traffic resumes; if it fails, the system waits and probes again.

quiz.explanation: Fault tolerance is the ability to continue operating correctly after a component fails — strictly, the user sees no error at all. High availability is a softer goal: the system is up most of the time (e.g., 99.99%), accepting brief periods of degraded or failed service.

quiz.explanation: The bulkhead pattern, named after the watertight compartments in a ship's hull, isolates resources so that a failure in one part of the system cannot consume the resources of other parts. In microservices, the typical application is thread pool isolation: instead of one shared thread pool handling all downstream calls, each downstream service gets its own dedicated pool.

quiz.explanation: Spanner shards data into "tablets," each replicated across at least three datacenters in different regions using Paxos. Writes are committed by a Paxos majority — typically two of three replicas — so a single datacenter failure does not block writes. Each Paxos group has a leader, elected by the replicas; if the leader's datacenter fails, the surviving majority elects a new leader within seconds, and writes resume.
